article_text:
Non più le penombre solenni dei musei archeologici, le teche isolate e i fasci di luce che sottraggono gli oggetti al buio. Non più la distanza sacrale del reperto. In Global Antiquity , progetto di ricerca a cura di Salvatore Settis , Anna Anguissola e Chiara Ballestrazzi , in mostra in Fondazione Prada Milano fino al 1 marzo 2027, l’allestimento di Rem Koolhaas e AMO/OMA sceglie di sovvertire il consueto codice espositivo. La luce è diffusa, lo spazio aperto, le teche non separano ma uniscono, mettono in relazione. Opere e artefatti si avvicinano non secondo una rigida successione cronologica o geografica ma sulla base di affinità formali, materiali e iconografiche. Oggetti lontani per provenienza e periodo storico in costante dialogo.

A emergere è un’antichità senza confini disciplinari, nella quale le somiglianze contano quanto le differenze e le distanze geografiche collassano al fine di rivelare una trama fitta di connessioni inattese. Qui l’archeologia non abita il buio ma lo dissipa e invita l’osservatore a cambiare postura: non più spettatore passivo dl reperti da contemplare in virtù della loro unicità ma osservatore attento di oggetti parlanti, parte di una storia più ampia, fatta di scambi, rimandi e sorprendenti corrispondenze.

Terzo tra i progetti dedicati all’archeologia da Fondazione Prada, Global Antiquity: Cultural Interactions in Afroeurasian Space, 600 BCE–1000 CE rappresenta una narrazione legata non solo e non tanto agli oggetti ma piuttosto alla loro de-gerarchizzazione. Un processo possibile solo grazie alla messa in luce delle loro origini, dei loro trascorsi e migrazioni, dell’interconnessione tra le terre, i popoli e le culture che li hanno generati.

Un processo di indagine che Salvatore Settis definisce “archeologia della luce”, capace di catalizzare storie e attivare voci altrimenti sopite. Come quella della statuetta femminile in avorio proveniente dal subcontinente indiano e rinvenuta a Pompei, dove era giunta prima della grande eruzione del 79 d.C. che seppellì la città sotto una coltre di cenere e lapilli. O quella di un Buddha ritrovato presso il tempio di Iside a Berenice, sul Mar Rosso: un marmo greco scolpito da un maestro alessandrino per un committente indiano nell’Egitto del secondo secolo d.C. e caratterizzato da vesti, capelli e aureola tipici della raffigurazione del Gandhāra.

Più che restituire un’istantanea degli usi, dei costumi e delle espressioni artistiche di specifiche aree geografiche in determinati momenti storici, questi reperti sembrano prendere parola per raccontare un’altra storia: quella di culture tutt’altro che impermeabili, di civiltà che non si sono sviluppate (né mai si sarebbero potute sviluppare) in isolamento, bensì attraverso un continuo processo di scambio, appropriazione e ibridazione. Ogni oggetto diventa così la testimonianza materiale di un’identità in movimento, il risultato di incontri, attraversamenti e stratificazioni che rendono sempre più labili i confini tra ciò che è proprio e ciò che è altro, tra origine e destinazione, tra appartenenza e contaminazione. Le severe teche in ferro crudo e vetro lo raccontano con grande chiarezza: scrigni permeabili nei quali l’ordine cronologico e geografico cede il passo a una tematizzazione fondata su archetipi ricorrenti e temi trasversali. E così un astrolabio Iracheno del IX secolo d.C. trova spazio accanto a un suo analogo andaluso risalente a due secoli dopo; un reliquiario d’oro afghano del II secolo d.C., proveniente dallo stupa buddhista di Ahinposh, è esposto in prossimità delle monete – romane e locali – che conteneva al tempo del suo uso; e infine il Leone Bronzeo che domina la città di Venezia viene accostato a un zhenmushou in terracotta invetriata risalente al VII-IX secolo d.C., quasi a suggerire un legame di parentela tra il grande felino simbolo della Serenissima e la chimera protettrice dei tumuli della dinastia Tang.

In questo senso, Global Antiquity supera i confini della ricostruzione archeologica per assumere una portata più ampia, insieme culturale e politica. Se la Storia ci restituisce l’immagine di un mondo antico sostanzialmente interconnesso, questo assunto mette inevitabilmente in discussione anche l’idea contemporanea di identità come entità pura, stabile e circoscrivibile entro confini geografici, etnici o culturali. Piuttosto, gli oggetti in mostra raccontano identità che si formano, evolvono e mutano nel contatto, che assimilano linguaggi altri e li trasformano, che sussistono proprio in virtù della possibilità di essere attraversate. In questo senso, guardare all’antichità attraverso la lente della globalità antica – e non della contemporanea globalizzazione – significa anche interrogare il presente: ricordare che le culture non si comportano né si sono mai comportate come compartimenti stagni e che l’ibridazione non costituisce un’eccezione o una nota a margine nella storia delle civiltà ma una delle sue condizioni più essenziali e fondative.

L’identità, sembra suggerire Global Antiquity , non è mai stata un punto d’origine da difendere ma un processo da attraversare. E la Storia, molto prima che la contemporaneità ne facesse un terreno di conflitto, aveva già dimostrato che le culture esistono non malgrado le contaminazioni ma grazie a esse.

article_text:
魔法使いの夜

劇場公開日： 2026年11月20日

解説・あらすじ

「Fate」シリーズのTYPE-MOONが2012年にリリースしたビジュアルノベルゲーム「魔法使いの夜」をアニメーション映画化。 現代に生きる魔法使い・蒼崎青子。昼は頼れる生徒会長として高校生活を送る彼女は、夜になると見習い魔法使いとして、同居人の魔女・久遠寺有珠のもとで魔術の練習に明け暮れていた。ある静かな雨の朝。学校に呼び出された青子は、山奥から都会に引っ越してきた転校生・静希草十郎と出会う。本来なら交わるはずのなかった3人の出会いは、青子たちの平穏な日常を少しづつ変化させていく。 キャストは原作ゲームに引き続き、蒼崎青子役を戸松遥、久遠寺有珠役を花澤香菜、静希草十郎役を小林裕介が務める。アニメーション制作を担うのは、これまでもテレビアニメ「Fate/stay night [Unlimited Blade Works]」や劇場版「空の境界」シリーズなどのTYPE-MOON作品を手がけてきたufotable。インターネット発の音楽ユニット「supercell」が主題歌「夜と青」を手がけ、原作ゲームのエンディングテーマと同じく作詞・作曲・編曲をryo、歌唱をやなぎなぎが担当。

2026年製作／日本 配給：東宝、アニプレックス 劇場公開日：2026年11月20日

title_original: Organic at 20: how the publicity firm expanded while holding onto its “scrappy underdog” ethos
editorial_title_zh: Organic迎来20周年：这家公关公司如何在保持“不服输的黑马”精神的同时不断壮大
editorial_excerpt_zh: 当卡拉·库克（Caragh Cook）于2011年辞去公关公司Rogers & Cown的工作，加入Organic Marketing新扩充的公关部门担任高级职务时，她从未料到公司此后会走上这样一条演变之路。

article_text:
When Caragh Cook quit PR agency Rogers & Cown in 2011 to take a senior role at the newly beefed-up PR division of Organic Marketing, she never expected to witness the evolutionary path the company has subsequently taken.

What she joined was a small marketing company founded in 2006 by Nick Leese, and part of Target Media and Communications Group (TMCG) owned by Rob Wilkerson. Cook now serves as the managing director of Organic, the Havas-owned global communications agency for entertainment, with more than 90 staff, and offices in London, Los Angeles and Sydney. The London team is 80 with a further nine in long-term freelance roles.

And growth is only part of the story. The past 20 years have also seen seismic shifts in film promotion, as barriers have eroded between publicity and marketing functions and between online and offline, and teams have fused to create signature events and sticky viral moments to drive consumer engagement. Work for streamers – which expanded significantly in the pandemic era – has naturally led to teams working across both films and series.

In the early days of Organic, film publicity was dominated in the UK by agencies such as Premier PR (which had absorbed McDonald & Rutter in 2006), DDA and Freud Communications. Premier’s Becky Palmer and DDA’s Kirsty Langsdale quickly joined the Organic team, alongside Cook and her fellow Rogers & Cowan colleague Emma McCorkell, who was named managing director in 2013 and left in 2015.

“We’d all come from very established agencies or in-house,” says Cook of the early team. “And we all loved this vibe at Organic that was just scrappy and underdogs, and we were all really hungry.”

Source: Peter Searle

Caragh Cook

Organic in its infancy won PR team of the year at the Screen Awards in 2012. “I think everyone else was a bit taken by surprise because we had definitely been underestimated,” reflects Cook. “It was an incredible vote of confidence.” (Organic went on to win the same category at the Screen Awards in 2015, 2017 and 2018.)

Tristan Woods-Scawen, with a marketing background, joined Organic in 2014, and now serves as general manager. The four-person executive leadership team comprises Cook, Woods-Scawen, managing partner Palmer and LA-based executive vice president Langsdale (all pictured in the main image above).

Woods-Scawen cites Organic’s growth in the fields of influence, events, production (with the recruitment of ITV Studios’ Nick Rylance in 2023), scripted and unscripted television, and its new awards division as examples of the company staying true to its original ethos. “It’s listening to clients. It’s being disruptive, and keeping that underdog startup mentality. Of course, it’s hard when you are a legacy PR business, and you’re part of a global media network – trying to stick it to the man is not easy.”

This comment from Woods-Scawen is underscored by the fact he and Cook are speaking to Screen in a meeting room at Havas’s stylish HQ in King’s Cross Central – rubbing shoulders with the Google campus, and emanating a different vibe from the company’s Soho origins. And Organic was able to celebrate its 20 th year with a buzzy party last week at Kettner’s in Soho, attended by clients, alumni and staff, including the LA team who had flown in.

For Cook, the acquisition of TMCG (and by extension Organic) by Havas in 2016 “brought so many brilliant things, like having an amazing office, being able to have great benefits for our team. It was quite limited what we could offer before. Now the team get fantastic parental leave, and a huge amount of support coming back.”

In expanding to a head count approaching 100 worldwide, Organic has followed an essential “recruitment tick list”, explains Woods-Scawen. “You’ve got to be expert, creative and nice. It’s very simple. If you hire someone that has those three things, you rarely go wrong. And the ‘nice’ thing is probably the most important of the three. It seems like such a soft word, but it makes such a difference.”

Adds Cook: “It’s why we have such longstanding relationships with our clients. Some of them are very long, and a lot of our former colleagues from Organic are now our clients. They get us.”

Organic Origins

Source: Organic

Origins: 2024 cohort

Many of Organic’s illustrious alumni return each year to teach on Organic’s Origins programme – an annual paid six-month internship scheme that particularly welcomes under-represented minorities in the industry.

“We’re not anti-nepotism,” begins Cook. “It’s fine to have people who have maybe come through connections – if they work hard and they show that they’ve got talent and passion.

“But more doors need to be opened to more people. We had a few moments where we’d go to meetings, and just look around the table and think, ‘How are we talking about this film by this filmmaker?’ and it’s this homogenous group of people making decisions. It just doesn’t feel right.”

The programme for five recruits each year combines practical experience (“giving as much exposure to red carpets and junkets and stuff like that”) with classroom sessions led by Organic team members and industry colleagues.

“A lot of the people who started their careers during Covid missed huge chunks as to why they were doing what they were doing,” adds Cook. “They didn’t have their teams around them, so it’s difficult to learn. The classroom sessions are about giving context to why they’re doing this.”

Eight current staffers went through the Origins programme, which launches its fourth season in January. Three more were identified through the Origins application process, but considered too experienced for the scheme and later recruited.

Awards division

Campaigning for film awards has become an increasingly important function for film publicity companies, but Organic has been out of the game since the departure of team member Bethan Dixon in 2014.

“When Bethan left, we kind of left awards alone,” explains Cook. “I think we felt you need somebody to be that figurehead. If we’re going to compete with the Premier or DDA awards teams now, we have to have somebody who knows their stuff, or certainly that can learn it very quickly. And we had other things to focus on.”

Organic’s new awards division is headed up by cinephile existing team member Will Taylor, with support from Anika Greblo, who joins from Premier. The team is working on titles for streamers, indie distributors and one studio.

“It’s been something we’ve been talking about since 2020,” explains Cook. “But then Covid happened, and we were like, ‘Maybe this isn’t the right time to launch an awards division. And do we really want to bring a whole other reason for people to have to work late?’ Our team works so incredibly hard during London Film Festival and this whole period from Venice through to Christmas and beyond.

“Will has been close to awards campaigning in his work with a particular client, so he knows what a good campaign looks like. We got the go-ahead [from Havas] to invest. They’ve got trust in us, and I think we’ve proved that we’ve made things work and paid off. Part of the reason people stick around so long at Organic is there are opportunities for them to evolve and grow.”

For contractual reasons, Organic does not talk about individual clients but Cook confirms that “we work with pretty much every studio, every distributor, whether it’s PR or events”.

Adds Woods-Scawen, “Since we’ve launched the productions team, companies we haven’t traditionally worked with from a PR point of view have knocked on our door, going, ‘We’d like to use your junket production.’”

Growing pains

With growth comes challenge. “We never set out to grow to the scale we are now,” explains Cook. “In fact, someone said to us a few years ago, ‘You’re going to have 80 people in a few years if you keep going the way you are’, and we were like, ‘No way, we don’t want to be that big.’”

But the growth has brough fresh opportunity. “It’s been exciting for us to see a client say, ‘Okay, we’ll put you on everything’” – meaning every aspect of a film campaign, from social to traditional media, talent handling, premiere and junket build.

Cook and Woods-Scawen remain mindful of not losing the ethos that drove the early success.

“It’s rolling sleeves up and getting involved and making sure that everyone knows that if there’s a mail drop to be done, I might be stuffing envelopes,” says Woods-Scawen.

“We’ve all come from doing the work,” adds Cook. “We’ve not parachuted into this role as a senior person. We’ve done the work, we’ve done the jobs, and we love it.”

article_text:
The Museum of Modern Art, New York publishes Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio , a sumptuous visual exploration of Brancusi’s art and studio through the artist’s own lens.

Over the course of his long career, the legendary sculptor Constantin Brancusi (1876–1957) created hundreds of photographs documenting the evolution of his artworks and the unique setting in which they were created. These luminous images capture Brancusi’s ever-changing studio across a span of more than thirty years, and range from intimate studies of individual sculptures to wide-angle views of carefully ordered ensembles. Striking scenes of artworks in progress, sculptors’ tools, and raw materials—including salvaged oak beams and rough blocks of marble—offer behind-the-scenes glimpses of Brancusi’s creative process. Photographs of the artist alongside visitors including Man Ray, Berenice Abbott, Marcel Duchamp, and Mina Loy show the studio as a lively space of work, play, and display.

Brancusi’s photographs bring to life his sculptures and his studio as he wanted them to be seen with extraordinary vividness and intimacy. Featuring more than 130 exquisite tritone reproductions of the artist’s photographs, Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio offers a revealing portrait of a dynamic environment that ultimately became a work of art in its own right.

Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio The Museum of Modern Art, New York By Anne Umland Hardcover, 9.5”w x 12”h, 160 pages; 266 illustrations ISBN: 978-1-63345-197-1 Price: $60 Publication date: October 2026

Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio is published by The Museum of Modern Art, New York, and available at MoMA stores and online at www.store.moma.org . It is distributed to trade through ARTBOOK|D.A.P. in the United States and Canada and through Thames & Hudson in the rest of the world.

The exhibition Brancusi: The Artist and His Studio is on view at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, from October 25, 2026 through February 27, 2027. More information can be found on our press site at https://press.moma.org/exhibition/brancusi-the-artist-and-his-studio/

Source: Maximilian Bühn, Wiki Commons CC BY-SA 4.0

Sebastián Lelio

The acclaimed Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio, who won the Oscar for A Fantastic Woman in 2018, has died. He was 52.

According to Chilean media reports the filmmaker was found dead at his Santiago home on Friday morning due to health reasons.

Lelio’s credits included Gloria , his most recent film The Wave , which premiered in Cannes last year, and English-language titles Disobedience , The Wonder , and Gloria Bell .

Trans drama A Fantastic Woman became the first – and so far, only – Chilean film to win the international feature Academy Award. Lelio was understood to be in production on his latest feature, Chilean Poet .

Lelio’s partner Amalia Kassia posted the news on Instagram on Friday morning. In a message in Spanish, she wrote: “It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of the Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio.

“We are going through a time of deep sorrow, and his memory will remain with us forever. He was a wonderful person who contributed to Chilean culture during significant moments in its history.

“As a family, we ask for respect for our privacy and for consideration during these difficult times.”

Sony Pictures Classics, who released A Fantastic Woman in the US, said: “Sebastián Lelio was a one-of-a-kind filmmaker whose work continued to evolve and surprise audiences around the world. His distinctive storytelling and singular vision will live on through a remarkable body of work that challenged conventions, touched hearts, and left an indelible mark on international cinema. He will be deeply missed.”

Her career is a testament to the value of pursuing a clear vision with dedication and consistency, and how such commitment can lead to meaningful achievements that leave a lasting mark on the global landscape of photography.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bin Thalith added: “Honouring creative talent lies at the heart of HIPA’s mission, inspired by the vision of His Highness Sheikh Hamdan Bin Mohammed Bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, and the Award’s patron. article_text:
French photojournalist Véronique de Viguerie has been named ‘HIPA Photographer of the Year’ for the 15th season of the Hamdan Bin Mohammed Bin Rashid Al Maktoum International Photography Award (HIPA), in recognition of more than two decades of work documenting life in conflict zones and societies affected by war, oppression and political unrest.

From Afghanistan and Yemen to Iraq, Somalia, Nigeria, Syria and Mali, Véronique de Viguerie has built a career capturing the realities of communities living through conflict. Her work looks beyond the violence itself, revealing the humour, tenderness, beauty, absurdity and resilience that persist in everyday life, even in the most challenging circumstances.

His Excellency Ali Bin Thalith, Secretary General of HIPA said, “Véronique de Viguerie’s work demonstrates the depth and impact that can emerge from a sustained commitment to photojournalism. Her distinctive perspective brings audiences closer to the human realities of places and communities that are too often viewed through the narrow lens of conflict. Her career is a testament to the value of pursuing a clear vision with dedication and consistency, and how such commitment can lead to meaningful achievements that leave a lasting mark on the global landscape of photography.”

Bin Thalith added: “Honouring creative talent lies at the heart of HIPA’s mission, inspired by the vision of His Highness Sheikh Hamdan Bin Mohammed Bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, and the Award’s patron. Through this vision, HIPA is committed to championing the arts, nurturing creative talent and supporting projects that make a meaningful, positive impact.”

The recognition carries particular significance for de Viguerie, who sees photography as a way to bridge geographical, cultural and human divides.

“This win is a great honour, and it carries profound significance for me. For over twenty years, photography has been my means of transcending geographical, cultural and human boundaries,” she said. “My lens has led me to places that are often misunderstood, viewed with suspicion and fear, or reduced to narrow, stereotypical portrayals.”

Reflecting on receiving the award, de Viguerie added: “As a European photographer, receiving this recognition from a prestigious Arab award is deeply moving; it serves as a reminder that photography is a universal language, one capable of building positive bridges that reach beyond borders and preconceived notions.”

De Viguerie added, “Throughout my career, I have always sought to look beyond the surface; beyond a simple black-and-white dichotomy, to reveal the colours, complexities and human dimensions that exist even in the darkest of places. The fact that HIPA has recognised this vision imbues this award with far greater value and meaning for me.”

The 15th season of HIPA is themed ‘Family’, inviting photographers to explore the connections, relationships and shared experiences that shape human life. The season’s winners will be honoured at a ceremony on Tuesday, 10 November 2026, at the Museum of the Future in Dubai.

The award reflects HIPA’s ongoing commitment to recognising photographic excellence and supporting visual storytelling that fosters cultural understanding and brings important human stories to international audiences.

About Véronique de Viguerie | France

French photojournalist whose work explores the grey zones of a world too often portrayed in black and white. For more than twenty years, she has worked in conflict zones and societies marked by war, repression and political upheaval, from Afghanistan to Yemen, Iraq, Somalia, Nigeria, Syria and Mali. Yet war itself is not her subject. What interests her is what survives within it: desire, humour, beauty, absurdity, tenderness, resistance and the rhythms of ordinary life.

Throughout her career, she has photographed places the outside world tends to understand through oppositions: victims and perpetrators, good and evil, freedom and oppression, us and them. Her work begins where these categories become insufficient. She is drawn to contradiction, ambiguity and the uncomfortable spaces in between.

Colour is fundamental to this approach. De Viguerie has deliberately worked in colour throughout her career, even in contexts traditionally represented through a darker, more austere visual language. For her, colour is neither decorative nor optimistic. It is a way of restoring complexity.

She does not photograph beauty in spite of war. She photographs beauty, desire, humour and colour because they, too, are part of war. To exclude them would be to create another kind of distortion.

This conviction has shaped her longstanding relationship with Afghanistan, which she first visited in 2003 and where she later lived for four years. She has returned repeatedly to document Taliban fighters, civilians, women, families and the profound transformation of Afghan society. Rather than reducing those she photographs to symbols the victim, the enemy, the oppressed woman, the fighter she seeks to preserve their contradictions and individuality.

Her work on women has become increasingly central to this vision. De Viguerie is particularly interested in women living within restrictive or violent systems who are too often represented solely through what is done to them. Her photographs instead explore what they do: how they negotiate, resist, love, organise, protect and reinvent themselves, sometimes claiming power in spaces from which they have long been excluded.

Her photographs have appeared in major international publications, including Paris Match, The New York Times, Stern, GEO, Le Figaro Magazine, Marie Claire and The Guardian. Her work has received numerous distinctions, including recognition from World Press Photo, the Canon Female Photojournalist Award, Bayeux Awards, and two Visa d’Or awards for her reporting from Yemen.

After more than two decades documenting conflict, Véronique de Viguerie’s work is ultimately not about violence. It is about resisting simplification. For her, photography is a way of putting faces back onto statistics, restoring humanity to those reduced to enemies or victims, and bringing colour back into stories the world has become accustomed to seeing in black and white.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位俄罗斯出生艺术家的最高拍卖纪录目前为4480万美元。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "俄罗斯出生的抽象艺术先驱瓦西里·康定斯基（Wassily Kandinsky）的画作《突出的角》（Betonte Ecken，1922–23年）将于11月17日在纽约佳士得上拍，估价为6000万至8000万美元。这位匿名卖家于1986年在纽约苏富比购得此作品。佳士得向ARTnews透露，该画作确定将以创纪录的价格成交。", "links": [{"text": "Wassily Kandinsky", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/wassily-kandinsky/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "康定斯基目前的拍卖纪录保持在4480万美元，该价格由其1910年的画作《穆尔瑙与教堂 II》（Murnau mit Kirche II / Murnau with Church II）于2023年在伦敦苏富比拍出。就在上个月，伦敦佳士得凭借其1907年的画布作品《多彩的生活》（Das bunte Leben / La vie mélangée）创下了该艺术家第二高（注：原文第三高）的价格，该作品以4150万美元成交，估价为3000万美元。该作品最近刚被归还给在纳粹时期失散艺术品的犹太荷裔收藏家家族的继承人。该艺术家的前14大拍卖作品全部超过2000万美元大关，其中10个价格是在过去十年中创下的。", "links": [{"text": "$44.8 million", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sothebys-london-sales-kandinsky-miriam-cahn-raghav-babbar-records-1234659424/"}, {"text": "sold for $41.5 million", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/christies-london-frieze-week-peter-simon-auction-results-2026-1234802435/"}, {"text": "recently been restituted", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/market/christies-london-offers-restituted-kandinsky-german-museum-1234796483/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这幅色彩缤纷的抽象画尺寸略超四平方英尺，其标题意为“突出的角”，是在德国魏玛创作的，当时这位艺术家正在传奇的包豪斯任教。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这幅画几经易手。佳士得的来源记录显示，它最早于1926年在柏林的雅各布·海希特拍卖行（Jacob Hecht Auction House）上拍，来自施瓦茨（Schwarz）收藏，随后进入该市的尼伦多夫画廊（Galerie Nierendorf），后者于1929年左右将其售予希拉·雷贝（Hilla Rebay）——她是美国抽象艺术早期支持者、博物馆创始人所罗门·R·古根海姆（Solomon R. Guggenheim）的顾问。古根海姆随后从雷贝手中买下此画，并一直留在该博物馆的藏品中，直到1964年博物馆在伦敦苏富比将其售予纽约艺术商斯蒂芬·哈恩（Stephen Hahn）。此后某时，哈恩将其售予波士顿收藏家桑德拉和大卫·巴卡拉（Sandra and David Bakalar），他们在1986年将其送交苏富比拍卖，并由此落入现藏家手中。苏富比未立即回复ARTnews关于该作品此前两次上拍成交价格的询问。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Wassily-Kandinsky-Das-bunte-Leben-1907.jpg?w=400", "alt": "一幅略带抽象色彩的画作，描绘了森林风景中的许多不同人物", "caption": "瓦西里·康定斯基，《多彩的生活》（1907年）。图片由佳士得提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "音乐对康定斯基的发展至关重要：1896年，30岁的他在莫斯科大剧院观看理查德·瓦格纳的歌剧《罗恩格林》演出后，放弃了法律与经济学的事业转向艺术。“在精神上我看到了我所有的色彩——它们浮现在我的心灵之眼面前，”据《纽约时报》报道，他后来回忆道，“狂野的、近乎疯狂的线条出现在我面前。这对我变得十分清晰，绘画可以发展出与音乐所拥有的相同的力量。”这段经历正是当前巴黎爱乐乐团举办的展览“康定斯基：色彩之乐”的核心所在。", "links": [{"text": "New York Times", "url": "https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/21/arts/design/wassily-kandinsky-music-exhibition.html"}, {"text": "current exhibition", "url": "https://philharmoniedeparis.fr/en/activite/28824"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“在这件杰作中，康定斯基实现了瓦格纳的‘总艺术作品’（Gesamtkunstwerk）理念，将他的创造力融合成一种单一、统一的艺术体验，”佳士得20世纪艺术晚拍联席主管佩姬·克斯滕曼（Paige Kestenman）在新闻材料中表示，“这幅画不仅代表了康定斯基自身艺术演进的新高度，也代表了抽象艺术发展中的一个关键时刻，它将影响后来的战后艺术家及未来几代人。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "康定斯基1866年出生于莫斯科，1911年出版了《论艺术的精神》（On the Spiritual in Art）一书，并且是具有影响力的“青骑士”（Blaue Reiter）团体的成员。在1912年于柏林施图尔姆画廊（Der Sturm gallery）举办首次个展后，他的作品之一入选了1913年纽约具有开创性的军械库展（Armory Show）。他在俄罗斯从1914年生活到1921年，主要在莫斯科，曾在人民教育委员会任职，直到1922年搬到魏玛。他的首场纽约个展于1923年举行，由马塞尔·杜尚（Marcel Duchamp）、凯瑟琳·德雷尔（Katherine Dreier）和曼·雷（Man Ray）于1920年创立的无名社（Société Anonyme）组织。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "康定斯基於1928年成为德国公民，但当纳粹政府于1933年关闭包豪斯时搬到了法国，并于1939年成为法国公民。纳粹在反对“颓废艺术”的运动中没收了他的数十件作品。康定斯基1944年12月在法国逝世，离他的78岁生日差三天，离德国向盟军投降差六个月。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Russian-born abstraction pioneer Wassily Kandinsky ‘s painting Betonte Ecken (1922–23) will come to the auction block at Christie’s New York on November 17, carrying a $60 million to $80 million estimate. The anonymous seller acquired the work at Sotheby’s New York in 1986. The painting is guaranteed to sell at a record-setting level, the house told ARTnews .

Kandinsky’s auction record currently stands at $44.8 million , paid for the artist’s 1910 painting Murnau mit Kirche II ( Murnau with Church II ) at Sotheby’s London in 2023. Just last month, Christie’s London notched the third-highest price for the artist with his 1907 canvas Das bunte Leben ( La vie mélangée ), which sold for $41.5 million against a $30 million estimate. That work had recently been restituted to the heirs of a Jewish Dutch collector family whose art was lost during the Nazi era. The artist’s top 14 works at auction all exceed the $20 million mark, and 10 of those prices have been set in the past decade.

Measuring just over four feet square, the colorful abstraction, whose title translates as Accentuated Corners , was painted in Weimar, Germany, while the artist was teaching at the legendary Bauhaus.

The painting has changed hands a number of times. Christie’s provenance shows it first coming to auction at the Jacob Hecht Auction House in Berlin in 1926, from the Schwarz collection, going to that city’s Galerie Nierendorf, which then sold it, probably in 1929, to Hilla Rebay—adviser to museum founder Solomon R. Guggenheim, an early supporter of abstract art in the US. Guggenheim later acquired it from Rebay, and it remained in the museum’s collection until 1964, when the museum sold it at Sotheby’s London to New York art dealer Stephen Hahn. At some point, Hahn sold it to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar, who put it up for auction at Sotheby’s in 1986, when it went to the present owner. Sotheby’s did not immediately respond to ARTnews ‘s inquiry about the prices the work fetched in its two previous visits to the block.

Music was key to Kandinsky’s evolution: he abandoned a career in law and economics for art after attending a performance of Richard Wagner’s opera Lohengrin at Moscow’s Bolshoi Theatre in 1896, at age 30. “In spirit I saw all my colors—they stood in front of my mind’s eye,” he later said, per the New York Times . “Wild, almost mad lines appeared before me. It became quite clear to me that painting could develop the same powers that music possessed.” The experience is at the crux of the current exhibition “Kandinsky: La musique des couleurs,” at the Philharmonie de Paris.

“In this masterwork, Kandinsky realizes Wagner’s notion of the Gesamtkunstwerk , synthesizing his creativity into a singular, unifying artistic experience,” said Paige Kestenman, co-head of Christie’s 20th-century art evening sale, in press materials. “This painting not only represents new heights in Kandinsky’s own artistic progression, but also a key moment in the development of abstraction that would influence leading postwar artists and generations to come.”

Born in Moscow in 1866, Kandinsky published the book On the Spiritual in Art in 1911 and was part of the influential Blaue Reiter group. After his first solo exhibition, at Der Sturm gallery in Berlin in 1912, one of his works was included in the groundbreaking 1913 Armory Show in New York. He lived in Russia from 1914 to 1921, mainly in Moscow, where he held a position at the People’s Commissariat of Education, until moving to Weimar in 1922. His first New York solo show came in 1923, organized by the Société Anonyme, the organization founded in 1920 by Marcel Duchamp, Katherine Dreier, and Man Ray.

Kandinsky became a German citizen in 1928 but relocated to France when the Nazi government closed the Bauhaus in 1933, becoming a French citizen in 1939. The Nazis seized dozens of his works in the party’s campaign against “degenerate art.” Kandinsky died in France in December 1944, three days short of his 78th birthday and six months shy of Germany’s surrender to Allied forces.

article_text:
A Japanese-Brazilian teenager forced to face a family loss nobody will talk about is at the heart of “ Yellow Chrysanthemum ,” the first feature from Japanese-Brazilian director André Hayato Saito, which is among the projects at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market .

The film is set in São Paulo in July 2014, while Brazil is staging the World Cup. Erika, 16, is a third-generation Japanese-Brazilian who feels like an outsider in the country she was born in and wants nothing to do with her family’s roots.

Related Stories

Disney Names Carol Choi Asia Pacific President as Luke Kang Retires

That rejection stems from an old wound. When Erika was 7, her cousin Yam, who was also her closest friend, vanished during a traditional festival in the Liberdade neighborhood while Erika’s mother was looking after the children. The family has been locked in guilty silence ever since.

Erika’s friendship with Bianca, a Black classmate mourning the recent death of her mother, stirs up the feelings she has long pushed down. Bianca makes no secret of her grief, and as the two girls grow closer, Erika’s family can no longer avoid confronting Yam’s absence.

“I vividly remember being a little boy, sitting in the bathroom with my father, when I suddenly asked him where we go after we die. He paused for a moment and answered with a long and profound silence,” Saito said.

Growing up in a Japanese-Brazilian household, Saito came to see how silence in his family could express love and respect while also hiding pain. His short films have dealt with grief, memory, identity and life between two cultures, and he described the feature as a continuation of that work.

One of those shorts, “Amarela,” also follows a Japanese-Brazilian teenager named Erika who turns her back on her family’s traditions, this time over the course of a World Cup final between Brazil and France. It competed for the short film Palme d’Or at Cannes in 2024, was shortlisted for the live-action short Oscar at the 98th Academy Awards and won best live-action short at Brazil’s Grande Otelo Awards. It is part of a trilogy of shorts, with “Kokoro to Kokoro” and “Vento Dourado,” that Saito made with São Paulo-based MyMama Entertainment.

“I don’t want to offer easy answers or a conventional sense of closure. I hope audiences will recognize something of their own families in Erika’s journey, regardless of their cultural backgrounds, and reflect on the things that remain unspoken in their own lives,” Saito said.

The project, a co-production between Brazil, Japan, Germany and France, is now in pre-production after several years of development. It took part in TorinoFilmLab, where it won the TorinoFilmLab Production Award, and was also selected for Focus Copro at Cannes. The team plans to film a key sequence during a traditional Japanese Toro Nagashi ceremony in Brazil in November this year.

Producer Mayra Faour Auad is the founder of MyMama Entertainment and produced “Amarela.” She has more than 20 credits, most of them international co-productions. MyMama is developing “Yellow Chrysanthemum” with One Two Films, Loaded Films and Blue Monday.

In Tokyo, Faour Auad said the team wants to close the film’s financing gap and connect with producers, distributors and sales agents who could carry the film to audiences around Asia.

“Given the film’s Japanese-Brazilian roots, finding an audience in Japan has particular meaning for us,” Faour Auad said.

Saito is also developing his second feature, “Little Faults,” which earned a spot in Turin’s Boost IT Lab this year. Its protagonist is an aging Japanese-Brazilian woman living in Japan who starts committing minor offenses, hoping to land in prison, where she thinks she might at last be cared for and feel she belongs.

The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival .

article_text:
In diesen Zeiten eine Möbelfirma zu gründen, ist mindestens mutig. Doch das Unternehmen Arwenn will die Deutschen mit guter Gestaltung und relativ zivilen Preisen überzeugen. Unsere Designkolumnistin fängt schon mal an zu sparen

Es sagt wahrscheinlich mehr über den Designstandort Deutschland aus als über seinen Wirtschaftsstandort, dass es im Oktober zu einer der spektakulärsten Möbelladeneröffnungen nach dem Zweiten Weltkrieg kam. Im Internet und in Berlin verkauft die Firma Arwenn seitdem etwa 60 Produkte – von der Wanduhr bis zum Sofa.

Bis auf die Lampen des Sortiments wird in Europa produziert. Und alle Produkte wurden von aufstrebenden bis etablierten, auf jeden Fall aber aufregenden Designern gestaltet. Gemessen daran, wie man in diesem Land die Kaufkraft seiner Bewohner einschätzt, ist das mutig. Aber gemessen am Interesse in diesem Land, es sich zu Hause schön zu machen und dabei nicht nur auf billige Wegwerfware zu setzen, ist das sehr mutig.

Doch die beiden Gründer haben eine klare Idee: Nicht exorbitant teuer und direkt verfügbar sollen ihre Produkte sein. Konstruktionen, Materialien und Fertigungsprozesse ermöglichen es, viele der Objekte flach verpacken zu können. Sie sollen einfach zu transportieren und zu montieren sein. Das erinnert natürlich an das schwedische Möbelhaus mit den vier Buchstaben – aber der gestalterische Anspruch sowie der ans Material sind hier deutlich höher.

Gute Gestaltung zugänglich machen

Diese Wette auf Deutschland als Designstandort gehen Möbelunternehmer Ruben Hutschemaekers, der mal für Hay gearbeitet hat, und Industriedesigner Sebastian Schönheit ein, der bei der Berliner Firma New Tendency gestaltete. Und vielleicht ist der Ansatz ihrer neuen Firma am ehesten mit der vor über 20 Jahren in Dänemark gegründeten Marke Hay vergleichbar: gute Gestaltung zugänglich machen. Und diese Gestaltung von Arwenn ist am ehesten mit New Tendency in Verbindung zu bringen, dem Studio, das 2012 in Berlin gegründet wurde, sich mit seiner cleanen Ästhetik in der Tradition des Bauhauses sieht und in Berlin überhaupt erst wieder so etwas wie eine Designbegeisterung hervorgebracht hat.

Das Aufregende ist hier also nicht nur, dass man die Kartons gleich aus den Regalen hebt und die neue Lampe und den Stuhl auf dem Fahrrad mitnimmt, es ist die ganz große Freude daran, diese guten Entwürfe kaufen zu können, die entweder im Studio von Arwenn entworfen wurden oder von Designern, die Arwenn anfragte, was sie noch so in der Schublade liegen haben.

Lebt die Friedrichstraße wieder?

Da ist zum Beispiel ein Stuhl vom jungen Berliner Moritz Walter, eine Uhr vom Berliner Studio Oe, das zuletzt einen Sessel für Vitra gestaltet hat, und eine Lampe von Relvãokellermann, einem international tätigen Büro für Industriedesign aus München. Es wäre unter anderem diese Lampe, die ich als Erstes kaufen würde.

"Solid" sieht aus wie eine Mischung aus Ziegelstein, Ampel und Kleenex-Box . Es gibt sie in Grün, Buttergelb und verwaschenem Weiß. Ihre zwei Leuchtmittel sind dimmbar, auch kabellos nutzbar, und sie lässt sich ganz hervorragend im Raum bewegen und auf einem Tisch platzieren, um unterschiedliche Lichtsituationen zu erschaffen.

Zur Eröffnung des Arwenn-Ladens an der Berliner Friedrichstraße kamen so viele Leute, dass man freudig dachte, dass dieses Quartier endlich wieder lebt, dort, wo sich in den letzten Jahren vor allem die deutsche Traurigkeit spiegelte: eine Fahrradstraße, die mal eine ist, dann doch wieder nicht, der Niedergang des Kaufhauses Galeries Lafayette, ein russisches Haus, das Angst verbreitet.

Ich spare mal

Aber nun gibt es fast genau daneben einen neuen Möbelladen. Und davor sammelte sich eine große Traube von Menschen, die sogleich diskutierten, ob das denn in einer Zeit, in der die Leute nicht mal mehr Geld haben, um essen zu gehen, etwas werden kann. Gerade hat die Firma Kahla Porzellan aus Thüringen verkündet, nach mehr als 170 Jahren ihre Öfen ausstellen zu müssen. Zu hohe Energiekosten, kein Investor zu finden.

Drinnen bei Arwenn erzählt Ruben Hutschemaekers dagegen von weiteren Läden in München und Hamburg. Frankfurt am Main und Köln sind auch geplant. Und schon jetzt gingen im Onlineshop jeden Tag Bestellungen ein. Und die Preise? Die Lampe "Solid" kostet 265 Euro. Das ist viel Geld, und doch viel weniger, als sonst eine Designerlampe kostet. Ich spare mal.

article_text:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on September 15, 2016 at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters on Friday, October 23.]

When I meet Alden Ehrenreich for breakfast inside a Toronto hotel, it’s way too early in the morning for this kind of music. It’s the kind of music that plays over the most dramatic parts of a movie. And it’s pretty loud. It’s the kind of music that plays when a character finally reveals the truth . I now needed Ehrenreich to reveal the truth , whatever that may be. This kind of music playing for us demanded such a thing, or what were we even doing here in the first place, except being slightly annoyed by it.

Ehrenreich is in Toronto in support of Anton Corbijn’s “A Talent for Murder,” which debuted at the Toronto International Film Festival earlier this week. He plays Edward, a representative for a New York City publishing house, who has been tasked with traveling to Switzerland to meet with Patricia Highsmith (Helen Mirren), to try and convince her to write a sixth Tom Ripley book. As things progress, very reluctantly at first, the pair start hatching a story idea that envisions Edward in the Tom Ripley persona. Ehrenreich points out this is a much more interesting way into that character than just it being “a Tom Ripley movie,” in which people would have their preconceived notions of what this character should be. (A path Ehrenreich has very much been down before.)

When I got to the restaurant, I didn’t know what to expect. Like, literally. I was just told “show up here at this time,” which at a film festival is really all the information that’s needed. But I didn’t know if this was going to be a quick interview where multiple journalists are shuffled in and out, or something more interesting to meet the dramatic music that was playing.

Over the course of 40 minutes, we had plenty of time to jump into a lot . From Ehrenreich’s recent Tony win for “Becky Shaw” (which I saw and was fantastic), his interpretation of his role in “Oppenheimer,” how he was told “Beautiful Creatures” would be the next “Twilight,” why he joined the MCU, and how and why he learned to stop reading about himself in the press .

Oh, and Steve Urkel. He had a lot to say about Steve Urkel.

When I arrived, I happened to be wearing a Mr. Roper t-shirt under a dress shirt and this immediately caught Ehrenreich’s attention and he asked about it…

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: The first day I wore this, a random superintendent in New York was doing some work outside and stopped me on the street and in a very serious voice said, “What a great shirt. You know, they never respected him.”

Alden Ehrenreich: Right! He relates to the super.

He relates to Mr. Roper.

He identifies as the landlord there. Yeah, that’s really funny. Crazy people with their sexual escapades. They’ve got to be stopped!

By the way, this is really dramatic music playing for 10:00 AM.

Right? This is not a room that you usually spend time in in the morning.

I feel like you need to say something profound because of the music.

Exactly.

Is it intimidating going head-to-head with Helen Mirren for an entire movie ?

We did a week of rehearsal about a year in advance of shooting the movie, and she was just so lovely. I’m imagining that’s the way she is in an interview? She’s so kind of gentle and warm and soft-spoken and funny and personable…

And opinionated. Yes, I brought up “The Mosquito Coast” to her in an interview and she had some very strong opinions about the critics’ reactions to Harrison Ford playing that kind of role at the time.

Yeah. She is. but she just lets the environment be whatever it’s going to be. I just immediately really got along with her and we had a great time. Before the movie was supposed to go, it all fell apart. And then we didn’t know whether it was going to happen again. Then it happened a year later. It came back and we shot it again.

Why did it fall apart?

Just financing stuff. It was wild, because when we came back it was like let’s remember what it was we were doing a year ago…

[Our server, Amy, asks for our orders and asks if we have any allergies.]

I get in trouble with doctors because when they ask me if I have allergies, I say cyanide and they get mad. I’ve never made a doctor laugh at that.

Really? They don’t like it?

They do not.

I think it’s good. I like it. When I’m at a restaurant and they say, “Do you have any allergies?” Sometimes I say cats, which is true.

See, I’ve tried the cyanide line once at a restaurant and I got the look of scorn.

Restaurant is trickier.

And I understand, because they’re busy and they don’t have time for buffonery.

Tomfoolery.

Have you ever been at a Broadway show and it feels like the actor on stage is looking right at you and it’s really uncomfortable? You did that to me in “Becky Shaw.”

Oh, really? You were sitting up front?

Yeah, we had press tickets. In a scene in which your character is seething with rage. It’s very uncomfortable.

That’s really funny.

I don’t know if you can actually see anyone up there.

I can’t. Not until the curtain call. Technically I probably could, but I’m not. I mean, I’m avoiding it at all costs. And I try to keep my sight lines on other parts of the theater where I don’t look at somebody, because you could look down at somebody and they’re looking at their phone.

Oh, that’s rude.

It kind of takes you out of it. Yeah. I mean, I didn’t have that experience, but you want to try to, in a way, see the fourth wall that isn’t there basically.

There were literal headlines that read, “Alden Ehrenreich steals the show.” You had to know things were going well.

I had wanted to do a play for a really long time. I had this weird relationship with theater where I had a theater company in my twenties, I’m opening a theater in Los Angeles at the moment, and it’s a huge part of my life. But I’ve never done a professional play.

How’s that possible?

It just is weird. There are ones that have come around that I didn’t want to do. There are ones that I pursued that I didn’t get.

It does seem like a huge commitment.

Yes, it is that. And you do it far in advance. So you commit to a play a lot. My admiration for especially older theater actors in terms of just the physical cost and in terms of they’re really doing it for the love. Nobody’s getting rich at all. And I saw people work a lot harder for a lot less on stage than I’ve seen in many instances in film. Finding that particular play and that role, there’s just once in a while you find a role that you’re like, “I can’t wait to say this stuff. I can’t wait to do this. I know I’m this guy.” I didn’t expect it to go as well as it did necessarily…

I doubt anyone goes into it thinking, “Guess who’s getting a Tony for this?”

No. I mean, I remember when I signed up my agent being like, “And it’s kind of during award season.” So I was like, “Oof, OK.” And it’s such an interesting thing because when reviews for movies come out, like today, that will happen. I really try to avoid it and all that stuff. But when you’re in a play, you have to avoid it because you actually still have to go do it . So you are taking this gamble. If you are in something and it doesn’t go over well, it’s not like you go, “OK, on to the next one.” It’s like, “OK, another six months of this.”

Right, if a movie doesn’t go over well, you can just say, “OK, I’m in ‘Oppenheimer’ now. Here I go.”

Yeah, exactly. And the way I’ve worked has always been a little bit like a theater actor, a little bit, the way I work on roles. So it felt like, I don’t know, it just felt like I got to come into an environment that was always kind of a natural fit for me, but that I’d never experienced before.

Here’s what I noticed: When you came out for the curtain call you weren’t smiling or anything. You still looked like you were in character. You took a quick bow and got off stage.

I mean, I got that note when we were in dress rehearsal. They were like, “Try to look a little less miserable.”

Miserable’s not the word. It’s like you were still the character. But you didn’t look happy.

Totally. The emotional climax of the whole piece for my character happens 30 seconds before the play ends.

I like that you didn’t take their note.

Yeah, I think what you said is probably true. I’m still kind of in it at that point. It takes a little bit of a moment afterwards to… Little rituals and get out of it and shift gears a little bit, which is its own process that I was learning through that whole period. How do you balance your day-to-day life? It’s very different. In a movie you have a big scene on Thursday, and the hours, they’re longer. With a play, you do the whole thing, obviously, you’re living the whole story every day. And so you have more downtime, but in a way that downtime is more needed for recovery.

So you went straight from “A Talent for Murder” to “Becky Shaw” on Broadway? Is that how that worked out?

Oh, no. I went back to LA and was writing, and then we did a play reading at my theater with Robert Downey Jr. of “Our Town.”

So you got to steal some more scenes from him like in “Openheimer”?

I wasn’t in it. He was unbelievable. He played the stage manager.

But you know you did that in “Oppenheimer.” You know you got some big laughs.

I love my character.

Well, he’s great.

When I did that, I watched “Mr. Smith Goes to Washington,” because I think for all the gravitas of that movie, there’s a lot of a brooding quality to the movie. And Chris Nolan never said anything like this, but I felt a, kind of, I don’t know… almost like an old school classical sort of patriotism in the writing that I felt like Chris Nolan was moved by and mattered to him. And that was something that I felt a lot of as a kid. And obviously becomes more complicated as you grow up and as the world changes and as the country changes. But to be in that moment and get to play a character that was very much the sort of, to me, kind of a character that was in the world of a Jimmy Stewart or a person like that was very exciting.

And you got to deliver the big line about JFK and act like you have no idea who that is.

Yeah, that’s true. You have to downplay that. And even that is almost like that line I felt he’s invoking a kind of optimism. Because even though now we’ve lived so far past that moment, what Kennedy represented, the kind of hopefulness and optimism that Kennedy represented is probably comparable, in some way, to what Obama represented when he first came on the scene. It was like my character was like, “Oh, there’s a future past this era that we’re all going to move into that’s going to be a lot brighter for the country.” I’m curious how Chris Nolan actually feels about that, but there was almost a sentimental quality in a movie that feels very unsentimental at its face.

You mentioned how you always wanted to do a play, and “A Talent for Murder” is based on a play. Was this scratching that itch before you actually got to do it? I know it’s not the same. You’re not in front of a crowd.

No, it’s not, but it is sort of? I think some of the things that draw me to theater are the things that drew me to the movie because, when I read it, and I knew that Helen was doing it, it was like a little bit almost like… so, I did a movie called “Hail, Caesar!” 10 years ago or something…

I’m very familiar with “Hail, Caesar!,” yes.

So I got to do sort of…

You have one of the most famous lines of dialogue in that movie that will follow you the rest of your life. I love it when actors do that, “I did this little Coen brothers movie, ‘Hail, Caesar!’ I don’t know if you saw it or not.”

[ Laughs ] I don’t assume! But yes, it’s true. And that line follows me in the good times and the bad times. There’s a lot of different ways to use that line. But that felt a little bit like, oh, I would get to do this one act play with Ralph Fiennes almost inside of it. And this felt like, oh, I get to do almost a full play with Helen. Anton Corbijn is not a theater guy, but me and Helen kind of rehearsed it in the very limited amount of time we had. The way we rehearsed all that stuff was very much the way you would rehearse it if it was a play.

Can we talk about where this movie goes or not?

It’s a good question. I don’t know the answer to that. I’m happy to, but it’s really up to the people.

The way I always look at it, if it gets more people to watch it, knowing a bit where it goes…

Sure. Yeah, I think so. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with talking about it.

As the movie goes on, your character, Edward, starts envisioning a sixth Tom Ripley book with himself as Ripley. Did you know this before you read the script?

No, I didn’t know the play.

So you’re just reading the script like, “Oh, wow, this is who I’m playing?”

Exactly.

What’s that like?

Yeah. I mean, not only that , but also doing it in this way. It would be a different thing if I was just doing another Ripley thing because then it’s a much more direct comparison…

You’ve gone down that road before.

Exactly . Speaking of “The Mosquito Coast”…

Good callback.

But this is so different, because it’s basically a novel that never actually got written, that we’re working on together. And I was talking to the writer last night about this. I feel that the Ripley in this movie, even though age-wise, I’m closer to a “Talented Mr. Ripley” era, the way she wrote Ripley in the movie, in particular, feels to me more like the later Ripley novels where he’s kind of just a sociopath, basically. In the early novel, there’s a part of him that’s very wounded and some of this is coming out of rage and all this.

By the time you get to the later novels, that has been all so repressed that he’s very comfortable with himself. So I think the opportunity to do two roles — and two roles that are this different and on this different kind of spectrum? I’m trying to remember other movies and things where that happens. I mean, I know there are ones. I guess the Urkel show.

Wait, are you referencing “Family Matters”?

Yeah, exactly. He gets to play the cool version of Urkel.

Well, there’s the headline.

[ Laughs ] Exactly. That’s just what I was thinking. That’s going to be the headline, “Compares this to Steve Urkel.”

“Tom Ripley, he’s just like Urkel.”

Not on Urkel, on Stefan Urquelle, or whatever, you know what I mean? The cool guy version. God, I haven’t seen that show in a long time.

Jaleel White.

Yeah! That’s right. I mean, yeah, it’s a very exciting draw to get to do both of those things at the same time and figure out how to do them. And we shot basically all the Ripley stuff first in Italy, in Rome, and then did all the stuff in the room. So I had the advantage of knowing what that all feels like when I’m in the contained scenes with Helen.

At the end it tells us this is a fictional account of her life. I assume for legal reasons.

Well, you want the real legal thing?

What is it?

I’m never referred to as Ripley in the movie.

So we’re getting someone sued with this interview?

Not exactly, because I’m just a Ripley-esque character, isn’t it? But there was some back and forth with that. And I understand the people who have the rights to the book, this is not canon, this is a whole other book. It’s a whole other thing. And so there’s a fine line to draw there.

I’m going to say something controversial, but I don’t even think it’s that controversial, but I’m going to make a statement.

OK.

In your life, you will play Han Solo again.

No idea.

If you look at the way history works with all this stuff, no one expected to see Andrew Garfield as Spider-Man again. Also, last time we spoke a couple of years ago, you mentioned you felt you only got to play Han Solo as the Han we know for only about the last 15 minutes of that movie.

Oh, interesting. We’ll see.

You also joined the MCU. Was your experience good?

I liked it. I’m pretty illiterate when it comes to the MCU and how it all works or where all that all fits.

Well, you’re Jeff Bridges’ son.

Yes, that’s true. I have to remember for a second. Yeah, and I just worked with Downey when I did that, and so I called him and I was like, “Hey, what do you think of me doing this?” He was like, “Yeah, do it.” He was very encouraging and supportive and stuff, which was very nice. Shanaka Hansch, who was the showrunner, I thought had a really cool take on it and it was super interesting. And yeah, it was a kind of very easy-breezy, fun, lighthearted thing. It felt different than a movie. You throw yourself into it in the same way, but I approach it the same way I approach everything. So yeah, we’ll see if I show up there again. I don’t know.

So let me word it this way. Last time we spoke, you mentioned that of course it’s disappointing “Solo” didn’t do better. But now, smash cut, there’s you holding a Tony, big smile, “Ehrenreich steals the show.” Professionally, do you ever think, “I was kind of in a disappointing place,” compared to now where things seem to be going very well for you?

Yes.

But do you ever take stock of that?

Yeah…

Were you ever like, “Am I going to get to a place where I can even win a Tony?”

Right. I don’t know. I wasn’t really thinking that at that time. I mean…

Look, I ask this because if something bad happens to me professionally, I’m like, “Well, that’s it. I’m done.” So I can only kind of ask that based on how I’d be feeling.

Totally. I think, for me, the thing that is the most… The only thing that I can have any control over is what I show up for, which projects I choose to do, and the way I show up for them, and giving them my all in whatever way I can. And if I don’t put a wall between myself and how that ends up. For instance, later this afternoon, we’ll get the Roman — whoever’s in the stands of the coliseum will do thumbs up or thumbs down on the movie to some extent.

Yes, that’s how it works here. Some guy comes out and does a thumbs up or down after.

[ Laughs ] Exactly. But that’ll happen today. I have other creative stuff that I’m working on. And if I get involved with how that goes, it just kills you. To some extent, when things go well, the same thing is true. It’s like you don’t have any control over the outcomes of anything.

Is this something you had to learn not to do? When you were doing “Hail, Caesar!” And “Rules Don’t Apply,” you’re in that era, were you reading more about yourself? Because you were up and coming then. I would be tempted to be like, “Oh, things are starting to go pretty well.”

I did a movie called “Beautiful Creatures” that was supposed to be the next “Twilight.” It was not the next “Twilight.”

No, it wasn’t.

I was 22, 23. Even my first film was one of the greatest experiences of my life, maybe. But even the way that movie ended up coming out, not the movie itself. The movie itself was great and it got great press, but then when it came out, it was kind of a non-event. And so it’s been a gradual learning over the years that that side of things is just not my purview. And how well things or how poor things go changes in an instant on both cases. The main thing, honestly, the thing that I feel that’s real is I just feel really grateful that I get to work.

I know a lot of actors who can’t work, can’t get jobs, never get to have experiences like what I’m experiencing right now — going to this film festival and staying in a nice place and doing all this stuff.

Well, you’re going to get an ovation for this later.

OK, that’s nice.

You’re going to get an ovation when you walk out today.

The only way I think I can stay somewhat sane is by really focusing on whatever the next thing is and on the things that I have control over. And that’s really it. Because anytime the rest of it, even when the rest of it gets very loud, it’s just not in my control at all. And the reasons that something are successful or not almost never has anything to do with… well, I don’t know if that’s true, but all you can do is your best thing. And sometimes that comes across and sometimes it doesn’t. And there is no lesson to me other than that, really, I guess.

I interviewed Courteney Cox a couple days ago . I noticed on her Wikipedia page, after the “Friends” section, the next section was called “Continued Success.” I feel like that’s a good goal. To have that listed after a main thing.

[ Laughs ] Totally. Totally . The thing that I also find really reassuring is that the artists that I really love, the people who I find very, very inspiring? It’s very easy when I’m 16 reading their biographies and looking back at the whole scope of their career…

Who would this be?

Oh, I’m thinking people like Marlon Brando or John Cassavetes, where most of their career is spent in… Would be deemed like failure or disappointment, or this or that, in real time. You look at that…

Cassavetes is fascinating. Because he plays these scumbags in some movies, but then he makes “Faces.”

Exactly!

It’s insane it’s the same person.

It’s amazing. And my sense of somebody like him is his entire… Whatever the headlines were in his era were certainly not about him and about his movie being number one or about this or that or any of that. And yet, over the course of time, because he was so committed to what he was trying to do, we have this feeling about him. Because over the course of time, the flame at the center of that stayed lit. And so the short-term gain of a certain success next week can kind of cost you the integrity of a lifetime sometimes, if you chase it. And then no one really cares or remembers anyway about how the thing did or didn’t do. It really is about the thing itself.

So that’s another kind of thing I try to remember sometimes. And it’s not like… I’m presenting this like I have this perfect… I, by no means, am not vulnerable to caring or having my feelings hurt or giving a shit about these things. But, as best I can, it’s just not really useful. And at its best, it can be instructive on how to keep your focus on the stuff you do care about or get clearer about what that is.

See, I feel you met the moment right there with the dramatic music that’s playing.

I did.

That was profound.

Appreciate it. The Steve Urkel stuff probably most of all.

“ A Talent for Murder ” premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. Bleecker Street will release the film in theaters on Friday, October 23.

article_text:
Selma Blair issued a video apology on Friday for the Oct. 11 incident in which she allegedly injured a flight attendant and kicked a nurse after being removed from a plane at John F. Kennedy International Airport.

Blair, 54, is facing two state charges of 2nd-degree assault for the alleged attacks on the nurse and a Port Authority officer.

In a video posted to Instagram, the “Cruel Intentions” and “Legally Blonde” actress said she had been advised by her attorneys not to say much about the case.

Related Stories

Ethan Klein Reacts to Hila Klein's Cheating Allegations Amid 'H3 Podcast' Fallout: 'Please Respect My Family's Privacy ... They Have Nothing to Do With This'

H3 Podcast Crew Cuts Ties With Ethan Klein After Hila Klein Says He Has Been Having an Affair

“What I can tell you, though, is very simple, and the truest thing I know about myself, and that not one day ever have I intended to hurt or frighten anyone a day in my life,” she said. “And so to the people that I disappointed, that I hurt, I frightened, alarmed: I am so sorry.”

Blair’s reps have previously blamed a “medical emergency” for the episode aboard the flight from L.A. to New York.

Blair was released from custody on $20,000 bail the following day. Blair’s attorney, Shawn Barnes, said in court that she had gotten on the flight after missing several doses of a drug that controls neurological symptoms. She also fell and hit her head during the flight.

“These factors, your honor, coupled with the altitude, resulted in a state of severe confusion and disorientation,” Barnes said. “Ms. Blair did not get on that plane intending for any of this.”

Blair is due back in court in Queens on Jan. 19.

"将小说家川上未映子于2011年发表的第一部恋爱小说《所有都是深夜的恋人们》搬上银幕，是由《东京贵族女子》的岨手由贵子担任导演及编剧的爱情片。由《惠子，凝视》的岸井雪乃担任主演，描绘了一名一直避免与他人产生关联的校对女性，在与年长物理教师加深交流的过程中，面对自己内心的孤独与情感的姿态。自由职业校对员入江冬子参加了同行聚集的聚会。然而，不擅长与人交往的她，根本跟不上周围谈话的节奏。当为数不多的朋友兼工作伙伴石川圣询问她平时的近况时，她只说自己过着没有亲密朋友也没有爱好的每一天，甚至连生日都是在深夜独自散步中度过的。而她这样的日常生活，以与年长物理教师三束的相遇为契机，开始一点点发生改变。主人公冬子由岸井雪乃饰演，物理教师三束由浅野忠信饰演，冬子的朋友圣由森田望智饰演，深川麻衣、盐野瑛久共演。冬子的独白旁白由松坂桃李担任。入围2026年第79届戛纳国际电影节“一种关注”单元。第39届东京国际电影节“Gala "未读过原著。在了解了校对这一工作的一面之缘的同时，作为一部细腻描绘笨拙人际交流的爱情电影，让人观后津津乐道。主人公是一直避免与他人产生关联的校对员冬子（岸井雪乃饰）。故事从她与年长物理教师三束（浅野忠信饰）的相遇开始推进。平时没有喝酒习惯的冬子，偶然走进一家酒铺购买了日本酒。以此为契机她开始沉迷于酒，甚至在社区学院里因为保温杯里的日本酒喝得太多而呕吐。三束恰好就在现场。这是在浪漫喜剧中绝不可能想到的相遇方式。字里行间充满了让人忍俊不禁的超现实描写，感受到了独特的韵味。令人印象深刻的是岸井雪乃的演技。她在街上收到的传单上写满校对符号，无论做什么都要请求“……我可以这样做吗？”。通过这些细致的举止，能够感受到她对工作的执着以及在人际交往上的笨拙。继《惠子，凝视》之后，再次被她的表现力深深吸引。据说岸井本人是原著的超级粉丝。她在舞台见面会上表示，正因为深爱原著，所以才不想单纯地照搬，而是想创造出电影独有的世界。从这番话中，能感受到她对作品的深厚爱意以及作为演员的责任感。与三束的关系也始终充满着生疏。对话公事公办，约会的服装和店铺的选择也全靠朋友的建议。在无法以真实的自我面对对方的情况下，三束没有出现下一次的约定。其中的原因，通过后来送达的一封细致的信件揭晓。有趣的是，两人这种擦肩而过有着一种不可思议的舒适感。一般来说，无法顺畅沟通的人物之间的故事，很容易勾起人的焦躁与不快。然而，岸井雪乃和浅野忠信之间这种生疏的互动，反而让人感受到了一丝温情。这究竟是为什么呢。我想大概是因为，即便彼此的心意无法很好地传达，但体贴对方的关怀，依然从表情和沉默的字里行间流露了出来吧。心灵相通与体贴对方，并不完全是一回事。正因为言语匮乏，才更能看到那些无法言说的温柔。这是一部在心中留下平静余韵的作品。", ホーム > 作品情報 > 映画「すべて真夜中の恋人たち」

劇場公開日： 2026年11月13日

解説・あらすじ

小説家・川上未映子が2011年に発表した初の恋愛小説「すべて真夜中の恋人たち」を、「あのこは貴族」の岨手由貴子が監督・脚本を手がけて映画化したラブストーリー。「ケイコ 目を澄ませて」の岸井ゆきのが主演を務め、人との関わりを避けて生きてきた校閲者の女性が、年上の物理教師と交流を深めるなかで、自らの孤独や感情と向き合っていく姿を描く。 フリーの校閲者である入江冬子は、同業者が集まる飲み会に参加する。しかし人と関わることが苦手な彼女は、周囲の会話のペースについていくことができない。数少ない友人で仕事相手の石川聖に普段の様子を聞かれても、親しい人も趣味もない毎日について話すだけで、誕生日ですら真夜中にひとり散歩をして過ごすのだという。そんな彼女の日常は、年上の物理教師・三束との出会いをきっかけに、少しずつ変わりはじめる。 主人公・冬子を岸井ゆきの、物理教師・三束を浅野忠信、冬子の友人・聖を森田望智が演じ、深川麻衣、塩野瑛久が共演。冬子の独白である語りを松坂桃李が担当。2026年・第79回カンヌ国際映画祭「ある視点」部門出品。第39回東京国際映画祭「ガラ・セレクション」部門上映作品。

2026年製作／139分／G／日本 配給：ビターズ・エンド 劇場公開日：2026年11月13日

原作は未読。校閲者という仕事の一端を知るとともに、不器用な人間同士の交流を繊細に描いた恋愛映画として楽しめた。 主人公は、人との関わりを避けて生きてきた校閲者・冬子（岸井ゆきの）。年上の物理教師・三束（浅野忠信）との出会いから物語が動き始める。 酒を飲む習慣のなかった冬子は、ふらりと立ち寄った酒屋で日本酒を購入。それをきっかけに酒にのめり込み、コミュニティカレッジで水筒の日本酒を飲みすぎて嘔吐してしまう。そこに偶然居合わせたのが三束だった。 ロマンティックコメディーでは考えられない出会い方だ。思わずクスクス笑ってしまうシュールな描写が随所にあり、独特の味わいを感じた。 印象的だったのは岸井ゆきのの演技。街で受け取ったチラシに校閲記号を書き込み、何をするにも「〇〇してもいいですか？」と許可を求める冬子。そうした細かな所作から、仕事へのこだわりや対人関係の不器用さが伝わってくる。『ケイコ 目を澄ませて』に続き、その表現力に引き込まれた。 岸井自身は原作の大ファンだという。舞台挨拶では、原作を愛するからこそ、単になぞるのではなく、映画ならではの世界を作りたかったと語っていた。その言葉から、作品への深い愛情と、俳優としての責任感を感じた。 三束との関係もどこまでもぎこちない。会話は他人行儀で、デートの服装も店選びも友人の助言に頼る。自分らしく相手と向き合えないまま、次の約束に三束は現れない。その理由は、後に届く丁寧な手紙によって明らかになる。 興味深いのは、二人のすれ違いが不思議と心地よかったことだ。一般に、意思疎通のできない人物同士の物語は、もどかしさや苛立ちを誘いやすい。しかし、岸井ゆきのと浅野忠信のぎこちないやり取りには、むしろ温かみを感じた。 なぜなのだろう。 おそらく、互いの気持ちはうまく伝わらなくても、相手を思いやる気遣いが、表情や沈黙の端々から伝わってくるからだと思う。 心を通わせることと、相手を思いやることは、必ずしも同じではない。 言葉が足りないからこそ、言葉にならない優しさが見えてくる。そんな静かな余韻が心に残る作品だった。

article_text:
The award-winning documentary Seized contains enough fascinating characters to pack a bingeable Netflix dramedy.

For instance, there’s Eric Meyer, the old-school journalist and editor of the Marion County Record , a small-town newspaper in Kansas; Meyer’s occasionally cantankerous 98-year-old mother Joan Meyer, publisher of the paper; and Gideon Cody, Marion’s police chief who conducted a raid on the newspaper office and on the home of Eric Meyer and his mother, possibly out of spite or to please his girlfriend, a local café owner named Kari Newell. A bonus character: Newell’s ex-bestie, Pam Maag, who had shared dirt on Kari’s dodgy driving history.

Related Stories

‘Everybody To Kenmure Street’s Felipe Bustos Sierra On “Small Revolutionary Acts” That Disrupted Immigration Raid – For The Love Of Docs

‘Ghost In The Machine’ Rings Alarm Bell About AI, Explores How Tech Is Fundamentally Biased – For The Love Of Docs

The difference, of course: this is no make-believe miniseries but a true-life tale that raised critical First Amendment issues. The stakes ramped up even more after Joan Meyer, the nonagenarian publisher, dropped dead the day after the raid. Filmmaker Sharon Liese lives within about two hours’ drive of Marion, KS and got to town just as the incident was making national headlines.

Watch on Deadline

Eric Meyer “knew that it was a canary in the coal mine story and he felt like if he was going to get justice, he really wanted the story out there,” Liese explained during a panel discussion about Seized that followed a screening of the film for Deadline’s For the Love of Docs event series. “I was really fortunate to be able to go there quickly. And since all of his equipment was seized [in the raid], he was not able to communicate with other documentary filmmakers at the time who were also wanting to scratch on the door about this.”

It didn’t take long for Liese and her filmmaking team to discover a long history of conflict in the town between supporters of Meyer and his sense of journalistic mission and other locals who felt he deserved to be toppled from his high horse. Liese calls the latter group the “anti-paper” faction. It fell to producer Paul Matyasovsky to get some of those Marion County Record critics to go on the record.

“Mike Powers, who is still the current mayor of Marion, Kansas, was not the mayor during the raids, was the first person that I reached out to,” Matyasovsky noted. “I’d seen that he had done a little bit of news media when [the raid] had first happened, but this was maybe six months now after the actual events and [we] told him where we were coming from on this project and feeling that it was important to not just hear about how everybody else felt, but to hear how they felt firsthand. At first, he was resistant, I’ll say, to the idea, but we talked and he came around and he was and is a very sort of well-respected figure in town. And once he gave his blessing by agreeing to be a part of it, other people followed from there.”

Another key participant, along with Eric Meyer and Mayor Powers: a cub reporter at the Record named Finn Hartnett who joined the staff after the raid. He becomes something of a proxy for the audience – an outsider to the town and its simmering feuds, animosities and differing perspectives on how a small-town paper should cover its leaders and goings on.

“We were really fortunate with the cast of characters that really we were given, because this was not a situation where you could go in and say, ‘Okay, who are we going to follow and who’s going to be our main person?’” Liese commented. “Eric was going to be our main person no matter what… And then Finn showed up and we were like, immediately, ‘We’re going to start the film with him.’ And then all the other people along the way that paraded through, I mean, we just had an embarrassment of riches in terms of the characters that we had in the editing room. So, it was amazing.”

Seized may leave many seized with laughter as the publisher and his antagonists butt heads. But the film by no means neglects the underlying significance of what happened in Marion, KS.

“It became clear that, and as we were looking for an editor, that we needed to imbue this film with a lot of humor because there was a lot of funny kinds of things that were going on with the town,” producer Sasha Alpert observed. “I think we did succeed in showing that this is a story with many, many sides, but in the end, love them or hate them, journalists are holding up a very, very important part of our society. And we see even now some very scary stuff going on when you ban journalists from the White House because you don’t agree with their politics or remove their offices from the Pentagon or whatever happened to [CNN’s] Don Lemon, et cetera.”

Seized won Best Documentary Feature at the Florida Film Festival and the Changemaker Award at the Woodstock Film Festival in New York. It won the Audience Choice award for Documentary Feature and the Heartland Filmmaker Award at Kansas City Film Festival International in Missouri – 150 miles or so from Marion, KS.

“We showed it in Lawrence, Kansas and in Kansas City [MO],” Liese shared. “People from Marion did show up to both of those and there was no picketing, there was no screaming at us. The people that came that wanted to see the film, I think really enjoyed it and felt like it was a fair portrayal, which we were really glad to hear.”

Watch the full conversation in the video above.

For The Love of Docs is produced with the long-time support of National Geographic Documentary Films . Films are presented free of charge to the audience and to the filmmakers. The series continues with weekly screenings, followed by conversations with filmmakers through December 1. Join us next week for The Life We Leave , directed by J.J. Gerber, a fascinating film about a man trying to revolutionize the funeral industry by introducing a new option – human composting. To RSVP for the screening, click here .

article_text:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good Morning!

A new study shows the UK art market remains the world’s second-largest in terms of sales, but its growth has slowed compared to top competitors.

Outsider artist Josef Hofer, who was hidden from Nazi forces by his parents due to a speech and developmental disability, has died at 80.

About 250 construction workers were evacuated on Monday from the Kanal-Centre Pompidou in Brussels as a precaution after a major gas leak nearby.

The Headlines

MARKET MOOD . A new study by Arts Economics for the British Art Market Federation shows the UK art market remains the world’s second-largest in terms of sales, but its growth has slowed compared to top competitors, partly due to regulations, reports The Art Newspaper . The UK art market grew from £2.6 billion in 1996 to £8 billion in 2025, making it the largest art market in Europe, according to the report. But since the 2009 financial crisis, it has been slower to grow, at just 17 percent since that benchmark until 2025, versus 114 percent in the US and 51 percent globally. “Overcomplicated and excessive regulation continues to disproportionately impact the many small and micro businesses that form the backbone of the UK art market,” said Thomas Christopherson, Chairman of BAMF , in a press release.

IN MEMORIAM. Outsider artist Josef Hofer , who was hidden from Nazi forces by his parents due to a speech and developmental disability, has died at 80, reports Le Quotidien de l’Art . Christian Berst ’s eponymous Paris gallery exhibited his last show this fall and told ARTnews via email: “He was one of those artists for whom creating was not a choice but a vital necessity. Drawing, for him, was a way of inhabiting the world, of making a mark in it and, perhaps, of inventing a place for himself there. His work, of rare intensity and humanity, will long continue to move us deeply.” In 1997, Hofer was discovered by art historian Elisabeth Telsnig, who gave a drawing class he attended in Austria. His drawings “represented a total break from anything I had been given to see until then,” she wrote in a catalog published alongside his last exhibition. Telsnig later helped connect him to institutions, and several exhibitions followed, beginning with the Collection de l’art brut in Lausanne (2003). The Centre Pompidou , as well as top collectors such as Antoine de Galbert, Bruno Decharme , and Arnulf Rainer , now own his work.

The Digest

About 250 construction workers were evacuated on Monday from the Kanal-Centre Pompidou in Brussels as a precaution due to a major gas leak nearby, as the new modern and contemporary art museum prepares to open to the public on November 28. [ Brussels Morning ]

Did the Mona Lisa struggle with chronic thinning hair, or alopecia areata ? That is what a dermatologist in Italy now claims in an academic journal. [ New York Post ]

Plans to light President Trump ’s 250-foot-tall triumphal arch with floodlights on six 30-foot-tall poles around its base could disrupt the darkness that is meant to cover Arlington National Cemetery at night. [ The Washington Post ]

New York City design studio AD-WO has won the commission to redesign the Carnegie Museum of Art’s Heinz Architectural Center in Pittsburgh. [ Artforum ]

Co-founder of MSCHF art and media collective, Lukas Bentel, announced he is breaking out on his own to “pursue solo work in art and design” and will collaborate with his brother, Nik Bentel. [ press release ]

The Kicker

NEW DEAD HEAD HOME? A new San Francisco Bay Area cultural center dedicated to Jerry Garcia, founder ofthe Grateful Dead rock band, is in the pipeline, his family announced, reports 24 Hip-Hop . The proposed center, organized through Jerry Garcia Music Arts entertainment services, would include a collection of archives, Garcia’s art and musical instruments. Exhibitions would focus on Garcia’s musical influence, his concern for the environment, ocean preservation, arts and music education. Though the project remains a proposal at this stage, Garcia’s family would also like the center to include an artist-in-residence program for visual and recording arts, a performance center and film-screening room. It is being planned in collaboration with the platform Starchive .
